clean_methods: To test whether bacterial translation inhibitors act through identical mechanisms in mitochondria as in bacteria, we will employ mitoribosome profiling in HEK293 cells to characterize the impact of a diverse panel of bacterial translation inhibitors on mitochondrial translation.

To cover distinct antibiotic classes and mechanisms, our approach involves treating cells with high concentrations of antibiotics representing different classes and mechanisms: retapamulin and tiamulin (pleuromutilin antibiotics that target the peptidyl-transferase center), josamycin and erythromycin (macrolide antibiotics), chloramphenicol and linezolid (context-dependent elongation inhibitors), and telithromycin (which causes context-dependent arrest at R/K-X-R/K motifs in bacteria).

To define the treatment conditions for detecting mitochondrial translation arrest, we will treat HEK293 cells with each antibiotic at concentrations of 100 µg/mL for tiamulin and josamycin, and 10 µg/mL for retapamulin, for 30 minutes, alongside DMSO-treated controls.

To ensure that mitoribosome-protected fragments are consistent and interpretable, we will optimize the mitoribosome profiling methodology by comparing RNase I and MNase digestion to determine which nuclease generates the most consistent and interpretable mitoribosome-protected fragments (MRPFs).

To evaluate the technical quality of the optimized mitoribosome profiling, the quality will be assessed through read phasing analysis, footprint length distribution, and coverage patterns across mitochondrial open reading frames.

To obtain mitochondrial ribosome footprints from treated cells, we will isolate mitoribosomes through sucrose gradient fractionation, where cytoplasmic ribosomes and mitoribosomes sediment in distinct 80S and 55S fractions respectively.
To identify sites of ribosome accumulation that indicate translation arrest, we will sequence the protected RNA fragments and map them to the mitochondrial genome.

To distinguish between initiation and elongation inhibitors, we will analyze the distribution of MRPFs across mitochondrial transcripts, expecting initiation inhibitors to cause accumulation of ribosomes at the 5' end of transcripts and elongation inhibitors to show context-dependent arrest patterns throughout the coding regions.

To determine the sequence contexts that promote ribosome stalling for context-dependent inhibitors, we will calculate the average change in MRPF abundance based on the identity of amino acids at the -1 (penultimate), P-site, and A-site positions.

To investigate translation initiation sites in mitochondrial transcripts, we will analyze MRPF sizes at the 5' ends of mitochondrial transcripts, using expected ribosome footprint lengths to correlate with start codon positions.

To validate alternative translation initiation sites suggested by mitoribosome profiling, we will complement our mitoribosome profiling data with protein mass spectrometry analysis of isolated mitochondria by detecting N-terminal peptides corresponding to different potential start codons.

To assess potential novel translation events on non-coding RNAs, we will analyze read phasing patterns and amino acid composition of putative open reading frames to assess whether genuine translation elongation occurs at these sites.
To ensure reproducibility and statistical significance of the findings, all experiments will include appropriate controls and replicates.
